name: Cork
lede: Cork is the light brown of the oak bark that stoppers bottles, and the same word once named a red-purple lichen dye and a bluish black.

sections.title: Which cork?
sections.body:
The word cork names three different materials in the pigment literature, and only one of them is brown [1]. The first is the bark of the cork oak, *Quercus suber*, a tree of southern Europe and north Africa whose bark is stripped from trees older than 20 years, then again every 8 to 10 years [1]. The second is the Amur cork tree, a source of yellow dye [1]. The third is a red-purple lichen dye, which in Britain was simply called cork [1][3].

The color word followed the bark. Paterson's dictionary calls cork "a beige colour", and the Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930 lists it on a plate of light browns [7][8]. The swatch here is that Maerz and Paul brown, which ISCC-NBS files as a light brown [8]. Sources disagree on how pale it should be, from beige to a mid tan-brown [7][8], so treat any single swatch as one reading. Nearby named colors are [[tan]], [[light-brown]] and [[camel]].

sections.title: The cork that dyed purple
sections.body:
In 1673 the naturalist John Ray noted that a lichen called *kenkerig* in Wales was known in England as cork or arcel [4]. The species is *Ochrolechia tartarea*, and its names ran through *korkje*, *corcur* and *korkir* [3][4]. Scraped from rocks with iron hoops, the lichen was steeped in stale urine to ferment, then mixed with lime or chalk and rolled into balls for storage [3]. The dye ranged from red through pink and magenta to purple [3].

A patent for the process was taken out in 1766 by Dr Cuthbert Gordon, and the trade name *cudbear* is a corruption of his first name [3]. Paterson defines cudbear as a red, violet, purple or brown dye from fermented lichens [7]. Cork was also used as a name for a dye from another lichen, *Parmelia omphalodes*, extracted by boiling water [4]. Mixed up with orchil, turnsole and litmus, these names confused writers until the nineteenth century, and the confusion is why a reader of an old recipe cannot tell what color "cork" meant without the context [4]. In our botany data this family sits under [[flower:lichens-orchil|orchil lichens]], and the red end of the family lies near [[crimson]] and [[magenta]].

sections.title: Cork black
sections.body:
Charred cork bark gave a black pigment, cork black, also sold as Spanish black into the 1920s [2]. The French writer Bouvier, in 1827, reported that his friends called it *outremer des gueux*, beggar's ultramarine, and said it was the bluest of blacks [2]. He found it weak in mixtures but excellent for white draperies, skies and distances [2]. The modern compendium groups it with bark chars, beside Swedish black from birch and vine black from grapevine [2].

The lesson for the eye is that a black can lean cool, and Bouvier's praise for skies and distances points the same way [2]. It is a reminder that [[black]] is a family of tones, not one color.

sections.title: Cork, the place
sections.body: Cork in Ireland gave its name to a different pigment, Cappagh brown, from a mine on Lord Audley's estate west of Skibbereen opened in 1814 [6]. Church's 1890 analysis found 34.4 per cent iron oxide and 27.2 per cent manganese oxide, which makes it an umber in the geological sense [6]. So a cork brown is the color of the bark, and the county's earth is a different thing, an [[umber]] [6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Cork is one of the commonest browns in our archive. In 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 2,908 of them, or 12 per cent [9]. The highest shares are in East Asian works on paper and silk: Miyagawa Choshun's *A Beauty Behind a Screen* (1745) has 89 per cent and Zhai Dakun's *Landscape* (1775) 86 per cent [9]. In those pictures the match is most likely the aged support itself, not a painted pigment, and the archive cannot tell the two apart [9].

The color rises in the 1200s and 1300s, with a lift of 2.5 to 2.8 against the whole archive, and peaks in the 1270s, when 21 of 48 paintings match [9]. Among painters, Rubens has 19 of 46 works with it [9]. Played in a picture it usually sits in the lightest tones, as a highlight in 65 per cent of cases [9]. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished works, so the colors are as photographed [9]. Next time you see a brown that looks like a wine cork, ask whether it is paint or a century of yellowing varnish and paper.

choices: A red-purple lichen dye and a bluish black

questions.q: Why did Bouvier call cork black beggar's ultramarine?
choices: It was the bluest of blacks and cheap
It was made from lapis lazuli
It was sold only to the poor by law
questions.answer: It was the bluest of blacks and cheap

questions.q: True or false: cudbear is a corruption of the name of Dr Cuthbert Gordon, who patented the lichen dye in 1766.

openers: Cork once named a purple dye: a lichen scraped from rocks and fermented in stale urine.
Charred cork was called beggar's ultramarine because it is the bluest of blacks.
